newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ may be ready to raise rates soon - traders.
newsitem.headline: BOJ may be ready to raise rates soon - traders.

text.p: Japan may be ready to raise interest rates in the fourth quarter, its first such move in seven years, if private demand keeps fuelling economic recovery in the next three months, senior traders said on Thursday.
Some even argued that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) has been quietly preparing for a rate rise by lessening excessive liquidity in the market from earlier this year.
Traders said that despite the BOJ's unusually accommodative market operations earlier this week, fears for higher rates after autumn kept three-month yen interest rates from falling.
The benchmark three-month certificates of deposit (CD) rate was at 0.67 percent on Thursday after hitting an 11-month high of 0.70 percent on Tuesday.

The BOJ's rate rise would be the first since 1990 following the severe slump in the economy following the collapse in 1990 of the asset-inflated economic "bubble." Rate increase rumours have circulated several times since then but have always come to nothing as the economy shows it is still in fragile health.

A senior dealer at a city bank said if rates were not believed to rise by the end of the year, the three-month CD rate would have fallen below 0.60 percent, given the key overnight call rate -- which banks charge to one another for overnight loans -- hovering just below 0.50 percent.
"But that is not the case for now," he said.
The BOJ stance has looked accomodative, matching the market's wide belief that there will be no rate rise in the summer.
That was also consistent with decision by the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Wednesday, traders said.
But some analysts say the BOJ is not being as generous as it looks because its net fund supply to the market through daily operations has been declining since late February.

"It seems that the BOJ has been taking precautiounary measures against inflation by not leaving excessive liquidity in the market," said Shoji Kitta, president of Totan Research Co Ltd, research arm of Tokyo Tanshi Co, a major money broker.
That was unthinkable two years ago when the BOJ started its hyper-accommodative monetary stance to support the slow recovery.
Kitta said that this suggests the BOJ is preparing for a rate rise in case of higher domestic prices, for example, due to the yen's fall against the dollar.
"The BOJ wants to avoid what it saw during the the economic bubble period of late 1980's when money spilt over from the market flew into stocks and real estates," Kitta said.

The most recent BOJ data available shows that outstanding BOJ credit to the money market fell to 971.4 billion yen ($8.52 billion) as of the end of March, 1997, which was less than 10 percent of the BOJ's net fund supply to the market a year ago.
As of the end of 1995, the balance of credit hit a peak of 18.2837 trillion yen ($160 billion) after the BOJ resumed to use an extra injection tool of buying commercial paper in November.

Since the BOJ cut the discount rate, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, to a record low 0.50 percent in September 1995, it has kept the key overnight call rate just below the discount rate on average by controling liquidity in the market.
A BOJ official said the bank increased its fund drainage operations recently by selling bills to the market. But he said that was mainly due to a seasonal fund surplus, which is to ease after July.
He also said the BOJ's outstanding credit is lower this year than in 1995 or in 1996 when there was a large market shortfall due to an increase in housing loans.
Commercial banks' lower lending rates than that of the government's housing agency at that time encouraged individual debtors to shift their borrowings.
"If the BOJ steps down fund supply now, short-term interest rates would rise very easily, compared with when the bank used to give ample credit to the market," Totan's Kitta said.
Apart from lingering fears of higher interest rates, CD rates were also underpinned by banks' strong demand to roll-over their 19 trillion yen ($166 billion) in CDs which matured in June.
